why: An OAuth2 connector is where the value-expression obligations all land at once, and every one of them is a rule nothing rejects: a `${...}` placeholder in a slot that takes characters literally, a ref path whose leading token patterns but whose tail resolves to nothing, a function name documentation calls planned, a token endpoint's value pre-computed instead of derived at connection time. Each of those produces a document that validates and then fails on the first real request. It also exercises the endpoint fan-out, which no other scenario reaches.
prompt: Build an API connector with connector_id xero for the Xero Accounting API, authenticating with OAuth2. Author the connector and an endpoint document for the Invoices resource. Do not ask me questions; make a reasonable choice where something is not stated, and ground every fact in Xero's own developer documentation.

assert.note: the auth type the provider actually operates, grounded in its own documentation rather than the archetype nearest to hand
storage is what routes an input into a connection's map; a client secret routed anywhere else lands in a tracked file

artifacts.note: presence only; the rule's content obligation is not graded
an API connector ships no Python package files

text_assert.note: a credential appears only as a reference expression into the secret scope, never as a literal
